title: Improve session cache stale file handling
body:
## Summary
- Filter stale cached session paths when the underlying file has been deleted.
- Prune deleted file entries from the in-memory session cache during cached discovery.
- Add a focused regression test for cached directory listings that still point at deleted files.

## Reliability rationale
This change improves reliability, maintenance value, CI confidence, or developer experience for the affected workflow while keeping the scope narrow and reviewable.
## Evidence
- `FindSessionFilesCached` can reuse cached directory listings when the directory mtime matches.
- Before this fix, `sortFilesByCache` trusted `cache.Entries[path]` without checking whether `path` still existed, so a deleted cached session could still be returned.
- The new regression test failed before the fix with a deleted `stale.jsonl` still present in discovery results, then passed after the fix.

## Scope
- Changed only `internal/engine/cache.go` and `internal/engine/engine_test.go`.
- No parser changes, no output format changes, no docs/marketing changes, no release changes.
- No new dependencies and no privacy-impacting behavior.

## Test plan
- `go test ./internal/engine -run TestFindSessionFilesCachedSkipsDeletedCachedFiles -count=1`
- `go test ./...`

Cline users could inspect local task history, conversation turns, tool activity, and session health in the same local TUI used for other AI coding agents.

## Adoption rationale
Cline has structured local history that maps naturally to agenttrace's compatibility surface. First-class import support would improve developer experience for users comparing or switching between local coding-agent tools.

- Parse `api_conversation_history.json` and `ui_messages.json` into normalized events.

Closes #32

## Summary
- Add Gemini chat/checkpoint wrapper detection for current local JSON shapes such as history, conversation, and checkpoint containers.
- Add bounded discovery for ~/.gemini/tmp chat and checkpoint files while skipping shadow Git-style directories.
- Extend Gemini parsing for top-level content arrays, function calls/results, thought text, and token usage aliases.
- Add synthetic fixtures and tests for current chat JSON, checkpoint JSON, malformed wrappers, and tmp discovery.

## User value
Gemini CLI users can inspect current local chat and checkpoint records without manually locating project-scoped temp files or reshaping JSON before import.

## Compatibility value
The adapter keeps existing contents/candidates parsing, accepts wrapper fields used by newer chat/checkpoint records, preserves unknown fields, and returns a clear parser error for unparseable Gemini wrappers.

## Scope
- Parser and discovery changes under internal/engine.
- Gemini fixtures under testdata.
- No README copy changes needed because Gemini CLI is already listed as supported.

## Test plan
- go test ./...
- go build -o /tmp/agenttrace ./cmd/agenttrace
- /tmp/agenttrace --doctor
- /tmp/agenttrace -f json testdata/gemini-current-chat.json
- /tmp/agenttrace -f json testdata/gemini-checkpoint.json
- malformed Gemini wrapper returns expected parser error
- /tmp/agenttrace --demo --overview -f json > /tmp/agenttrace-parser-after.json

## Safety checklist
- [x] Read-only local discovery only.
- [x] Does not restore checkpoints or inspect shadow Git contents.
- [x] No real prompts, sessions, tokens, secrets, or logs uploaded.
- [x] No new dependencies.
- [x] No protected files, release config, or workflow files changed.

title: [AgentOps] Improve Parser Builder prompt for stale branch conflict recovery
body:
## Background
Parser Builder currently has an open parser PR that passed CI but is no longer mergeable after upstream parser work landed. The same open parser PR has no linked GitHub issue, which weakens GitHub-first coordination and makes rebase/blocker ownership less clear.

## Evidence
- PR #21 `Add Cursor JSON value parser support`: `mergeStateStatus=DIRTY`, label `status/blocked`, CI check `Test and build` is green.
- Quality Gatekeeper comment on PR #21 at 2026-05-03T06:59:33Z: blocked because GitHub reports `mergeStateStatus=DIRTY`; requested rebase or merge latest `master`, conflict resolution, and rerun checks.
- `gh pr view 21 --json closingIssuesReferences` returned an empty array.
- Open parser PR #18 is green and `status/ready-for-merge`, but `closingIssuesReferences` is also empty.

## Root cause
The Parser Builder prompt does not make final mergeability and issue linkage a hard pre-review gate. It allows parser PRs to remain review-ready after adjacent parser merges make the branch stale, and it allows self-contained parser work without an explicit GitHub issue link.

## Suggested prompt change
Add this rule to the Parser Builder prompt:

```text
Before marking any parser PR ready for review or merge:
1. Fetch the latest `master` and update the branch by rebase or merge.
2. Run `gh pr view <PR> --json mergeStateStatus,statusCheckRollup,closingIssuesReferences`.
3. If `mergeStateStatus` is `DIRTY`, `BLOCKED`, or not clearly clean, do not request ready-for-merge. Comment the blocker, update labels to blocked/needs-changes, resolve the conflict, and rerun `go test ./...`, `go build`, and `agenttrace --doctor`.
4. Every parser PR must close or reference exactly one GitHub issue unless a human maintainer explicitly approves a self-contained PR.
5. After any upstream parser PR merges, re-check mergeability before asking Quality to pass the gate.
```

## Expected effect
Parser PRs should spend less time in green-but-unmergeable state, Quality review comments should point to a clear owner/action, and parser work should stay linked to GitHub issues as the coordination source of truth.

## Non-goals
Do not change parser code from this issue. Do not merge, rebase, or close PR #21 from this issue. Do not create release or community-facing copy.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Prompt rule updated
- [ ] Future PR/Issue behavior no longer reproduces this issue
- [ ] No public Star-target wording
- [ ] GitHub remains the collaboration source of truth

title: [AgentOps] Improve Growth & Release prompt for protected launch doc scope
body:
## Background
Growth & Release opened a launch/community-facing documentation PR without a linked issue or explicit human approval. Quality later blocked it as a protected surface, and the PR was closed without merge.

## Evidence
- PR #26 `Improve launch channel messaging` changed only `docs/launch-kit.md`.
- PR #26 had no linked issue and `gh pr view 26 --json closingIssuesReferences` is empty by body/link inspection.
- Quality Gatekeeper comment at 2026-05-03T06:42:45Z marked PR #26 BLOCK because `docs/launch-kit.md` is a protected launch and community-facing draft surface.
- PR #26 was closed at 2026-05-03T06:44:05Z with a comment saying the work should wait for an explicit linked issue or human maintainer approval.

## Root cause
The Growth & Release prompt does not clearly separate routine docs wording from protected launch/community-facing drafts. It also does not require a GitHub issue or explicit maintainer approval before touching public launch surfaces.

## Suggested prompt change
Add this rule to the Growth & Release prompt:

```text
Before opening any Growth PR, classify the changed files.
Protected public surfaces include `docs/launch-kit.md`, release notes, community/social drafts, SECURITY.md, PRIVACY.md, LICENSE, install/release automation, and any public announcement copy.
For protected public surfaces:
1. Do not open a PR unless there is a linked GitHub issue with explicit maintainer approval or `status/ready-for-agent` for that exact scope.
2. The PR body must include `Closes #<issue>` or `Refs #<issue>` and explain why the public copy improves User value, Developer experience, Adoption rationale, Maintenance value, or Workflow efficiency.
3. Keep all external posting manual. Do not publish social/community content.
4. If approval is missing, create or update a GitHub issue instead of changing the protected file.
```

## Expected effect
Growth work should avoid closed PR churn on protected public surfaces, make approval boundaries explicit, and keep community-facing changes reviewable through GitHub issues first.

## Non-goals
Do not reopen PR #26 from this issue. Do not edit launch copy, release notes, protected files, or community drafts here. Do not publish external content.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Prompt rule updated
- [ ] Future PR/Issue behavior no longer reproduces this issue
- [ ] No public Star-target wording
- [ ] GitHub remains the collaboration source of truth

title: [AgentOps] Improve Quality Gatekeeper prompt for protected doc gating
body:
## Background
Quality Gatekeeper initially passed a protected launch/community-facing documentation PR as self-contained, then later blocked the same PR. The later block was correct, but the first PASS created a window where protected public copy could have been treated as ready for merge.

## Evidence
- PR #26 `Improve launch channel messaging` changed `docs/launch-kit.md`.
- Quality Gatekeeper comment at 2026-05-03T06:15:20Z marked PR #26 PASS and noted no linked issue was found, treating it as a self-contained PR scope.
- Quality Gatekeeper comment at 2026-05-03T06:42:45Z changed the verdict to BLOCK because `docs/launch-kit.md` is a protected launch/community-facing draft surface and lacked explicit human maintainer approval.
- PR #26 was closed without merge at 2026-05-03T06:44:05Z.

## Root cause
The Quality Gatekeeper prompt allows broad self-contained PR approval before checking protected public surfaces and linked-issue requirements. The protected-file gate should run before general scope/test checks, not after a PASS comment has already been posted.

## Suggested prompt change
Add this rule to the Quality Gatekeeper prompt:

```text
Run protected-surface checks before any PASS verdict.
1. Inspect changed files first.
2. If the PR touches protected public surfaces such as `docs/launch-kit.md`, release notes, community/social drafts, SECURITY.md, PRIVACY.md, LICENSE, install/release automation, or external announcement copy, require a linked GitHub issue plus explicit maintainer approval for that exact scope.
3. Do not classify protected-surface PRs as self-contained.
4. If approval or issue linkage is missing, verdict must be BLOCK or NEEDS_CHANGES even when CI, build, and tests pass.
5. Every review comment must include linked-issue status, protected-surface status, mergeability, and CI status.
```

## Expected effect
Quality review should block protected public-surface risk before a PASS label/comment appears, reduce contradictory review signals, and make merge readiness easier for maintainers to trust.

## Non-goals
Do not change Quality code or workflow automation from this issue. Do not merge or reopen PR #26. Do not edit protected public files here.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Prompt rule updated
- [ ] Future PR/Issue behavior no longer reproduces this issue
- [ ] No public Star-target wording
- [ ] GitHub remains the collaboration source of truth

title: [Radar] Track Codex CLI usage and stuck-session evidence
body:
## Background

Public Codex CLI signals point to recurring needs around local session diagnostics: users want clearer usage/cost visibility, better progress feedback when the agent appears stuck, and usable evidence from local logs without uploading private session content.

## Evidence

- Tavily scan found Codex CLI diagnostic-log discussion around local logs such as `~/.codex/log/codex-tui.log`, including timestamps, request IDs, errors, and connection state.
- Tavily scan found public Codex CLI requests for status-line usage visibility and built-in cost/usage analytics.
- Tavily scan found multiple public Codex CLI reports of long-running or indefinite "Working" states across models/platforms.
- Current agenttrace product positioning already emphasizes local-first session observability, tool failures, token/cost burn, hanging gaps, and CI evidence.

## User value

Codex CLI users should be able to tell whether a session is making progress, burning tokens, waiting on tools, or failing silently, using local evidence they can inspect before sharing anything externally.

## Adoption rationale

Codex CLI compatibility is a strong developer-experience fit because the pain is close to agenttrace's existing value: local diagnostics, usage visibility, hanging-session detection, and privacy-preserving evidence.

## Suggested scope

- Confirm which current Codex CLI files are stable enough to document or parse for usage and hang diagnostics.
- Identify whether existing agenttrace Codex parsing already covers the relevant fields.
- Collect or synthesize safe fixtures that do not contain private prompts, session content, tokens, or credentials.
- Decide whether the next task should route to `lane/parser`, `lane/quality`, or remain radar-only.

## Non-goals

- Do not upload real user Codex sessions or logs.
- Do not change parser behavior until the local file shape and safe fixture strategy are confirmed.
- Do not make claims about full Codex CLI telemetry coverage without validation.
- Do not create external posts or release notes from this issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- A maintainer or radar agent identifies the relevant Codex CLI local files and fields.
- Existing agenttrace Codex coverage is checked against the observed fields.
- A safe fixture plan is documented if parser or quality work is needed.
- Follow-up work, if any, is routed with a concrete lane and acceptance criteria.

## Suggested lane

lane/radar, priority/P2, status/needs-human

## Risk

title: [Radar] Track Continue CLI session JSON parser readiness
body:
## Background
Continue now has a CLI and VS Code ecosystem surface with local session persistence. This is adjacent to agenttrace's local-first parser surface, but the exact fixture shape and privacy boundaries should be confirmed before turning it into parser implementation work.

## Evidence
- Tavily search found current Continue CLI and VS Code ecosystem references, including local IDE use and SQLite/indexing issues around `~/.continue/index`.
- `continuedev/continue` repository metadata shows an active developer-tool project with CLI and IDE extension topics.
- `core/util/paths.ts` defines the global Continue directory as `~/.continue` by default and creates a `sessions` directory under it.
- `core/util/paths.ts` exposes `getSessionFilePath(sessionId)` as `<sessions>/<sessionId>.json` and `getSessionsListPath()` as `<sessions>/sessions.json`.
- `extensions/cli/src/session.ts` creates UUID-based sessions with `workspaceDirectory`, `history`, and `usage` fields including cost and token counts.
- `core/util/history.ts` saves ordered session JSON files and updates `sessions.json` metadata with message counts.
- Duplicate check: `gh issue list --repo luoyuctl/agenttrace --search "continuedev sessions" --limit 1000` returned no existing issue.

## User value
Continue users could eventually inspect local CLI sessions, token usage, cost, and message history health without uploading private project context.

## Adoption rationale
Continue is a visible open-source AI coding tool with local session artifacts, so compatibility research could improve parser coverage and developer experience for users comparing multiple coding-agent workflows.

## Suggested scope
- Confirm current Continue CLI session file shape from public code and a sanitized fixture.
- Identify fields that are safe to parse, redact, or ignore, especially prompts, workspace paths, tool payloads, and remote-session metadata.
- Decide whether the format has enough stable evidence to promote into a parser issue.
- Record expected path defaults and the `CONTINUE_GLOBAL_DIR` override behavior.

## Non-goals
- Do not implement a parser in this issue.
- Do not read or upload private `~/.continue/sessions` files.
- Do not infer VS Code chat storage support from CLI session storage without separate evidence.
- Do not change README or release copy from this issue.

## Acceptance criteria
- Current Continue CLI session storage path and JSON shape are documented from public sources or sanitized fixtures.
- Sensitive fields and redaction expectations are listed.
- A clear go/no-go recommendation is made for a follow-up parser task.
- Any follow-up parser issue links this research and includes a minimal redacted fixture plan.

## Suggested lane
lane/radar, priority/P2, status/needs-human

## Risk
Continue storage may change quickly, and session JSON can include prompts, workspace paths, or tool context. Parser work should stay read-only and fixture-driven until the privacy boundary is clear.

## Source

- https://github.com/continuedev/continue/blob/main/extensions/cli/src/session.ts

title: [Radar] Track silent tool-success audit trail signal
body:
## Background
A public reliability signal describes an AI coding session where a write-like tool reported success, but the expected files were not present on disk. Recovery depended on having the session audit log available.

This is adjacent to agenttrace's anomaly and tool-result model, but it needs more evidence before becoming parser or quality implementation work. The core question is whether local session traces can help users identify "reported success, missing artifact" patterns without creating noisy false positives.

## Evidence
- Tavily scan found a public post describing a Claude Code session where write operations appeared successful in the tool transcript, but the files did not exist on disk. The author recovered from a large JSONL audit trail and emphasized independent verification of material AI actions.
- Current agenttrace demo already surfaces tool failures and anomalies, but silent-success cases may not appear as ordinary tool failures if the tool result itself claims success.

Source links:
- https://www.linkedin.com/posts/david-murfet-3390761_yesterday-claude-code-spent-hours-writing-activity-7450821564461252608-UKo4

## User value
Users get a path to investigate high-risk agent failures where the transcript looks successful but the expected project artifact is missing.

## Adoption rationale
Reliability value is strongest when local traces help users trust, audit, or challenge agent outcomes with evidence instead of relying on the assistant's own claim.

## Suggested scope
- Keep this as radar until at least one reproducible local fixture or additional public signal exists.
- Evaluate whether a future heuristic could compare successful write-like tool results with local file existence or final workspace state.
- Document the limitation if agenttrace can only show the transcript evidence and cannot independently verify the filesystem outcome.

## Non-goals
- No agent behavior modification.
- No external log upload.
- No broad filesystem scanning beyond explicit local user context.
- No implementation work until false-positive risk is understood.

## Acceptance criteria
- Collect at least one additional verified signal or a local reproducible fixture.
- Decide whether this belongs in lane/quality, lane/parser, or stays as documentation guidance.
- If promoted, define a narrow heuristic with clear privacy and false-positive boundaries.
- If not promoted, document why current tool-result evidence is insufficient.

## Suggested lane
lane/radar

## Risk
Medium. Silent-success detection can be valuable, but naive file checks could produce noisy results for generated paths, moved files, temporary files, or tools with virtualized write behavior.

Recent ecosystem discussion increasingly separates durable session traces from the model's active context window. Adjacent tools are framing verbose tool output, MCP/tool schemas, and compaction loss as developer-experience risks that need explicit routing or sandboxing.

Source links:
- https://github.com/mksglu/context-mode
- https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents
- https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47712718

## User value
Users can better understand when a session degraded because tool output volume or compaction pressure polluted the working context, instead of treating all failures as model quality issues.

## Adoption rationale
This strengthens local-first reliability value: agenttrace can remain an evidence layer that helps developers reason about context pressure, tool-output noise, and session continuity without uploading private logs.

## Suggested scope
- Keep this as radar until concrete local fixtures or repeated user reports exist.
- Compare current agenttrace fields against context-pressure symptoms: large token jumps, repeated reads, tool-heavy loops, long gaps, and compaction-related session boundaries where available.

title: [codex] Improve and verify TUI first-screen triage
body:
## Summary

- Add a first-screen `TRIAGE NOW` panel that shows the highest-risk session, issue, impact, evidence, key path, and next fix action.

The gap is not framework-level. Bubble Tea remains sufficient. The important benchmark gap was product UX and verification: top TUIs make the first screen answer "what do I do next?", and their core flows are easy to validate. This PR moves that into the overview and exposes the same TUI rendering path through CLI snapshots for CI and PR review.

## Headless TUI Verification Examples
`agenttrace --demo --tui-view all --tui-no-color`
`agenttrace --demo --tui-view detail --tui-command critical --tui-width 120 --tui-height 36`
`agenttrace --demo --tui-view overview --tui-keys '!;enter' --tui-no-color`

## Validation
- go test ./internal/tui -run 'TestRenderSnapshot|TestDetailRendersDiagnosticSummary|TestViewsRenderWithinTerminalWidth' -count=1 -v
- go test ./... -count=1
- go vet ./...

title: [Radar] Track active session management vs diagnostic positioning
body:
## Background

Public AI coding tooling is increasingly framing value around active session management: launching sessions, watching live output, resuming stalled work, approving diffs, and managing agents from another device. This is adjacent to agenttrace, but it is not the same user promise as local diagnostic reporting over existing session logs.

## Evidence

- OctoAlly positions itself as an AI coding session orchestration dashboard for Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, with active sessions grid, live streaming output, tmux-backed terminals, git diffs, and SQLite-backed state.
- Nimbalyst positions around mobile management for Claude Code and Codex sessions, including review diffs, resume stalled sessions, push notifications, and starting sessions from phone.
- Happy Coder docs describe remote/mobile control for Claude Code and Codex sessions, including starting sessions, approving changes, and checking long-running work from another device.

## User value

Users with long-running or multi-agent coding work want to know what is running, whether it is stuck, and how to re-enter or approve work without losing context.

## Adoption rationale

agenttrace should keep its adoption path clear: fast local evidence, diagnostics, tool failure visibility, health scoring, and shareable reports. The product can acknowledge active-session tools as adjacent without becoming an orchestrator.

## Suggested scope

- Treat active session management as a positioning boundary in radar.
- Use this evidence when refining README, Roadmap, and TUI first-screen copy.
- Emphasize post-run or local-log triage: tool failures, hanging gaps, high-cost sessions, health score, JSON/HTML artifacts.
- Consider future compatibility only where active tools leave local session logs that agenttrace can inspect read-only.

## Non-goals

- Do not add mobile control.
- Do not launch, resume, or approve coding-agent sessions.
- Do not add terminal multiplexing, git commit flows, or orchestration workflows.
- Do not upload session contents or depend on hosted coordination.

## Acceptance criteria

- The radar decision is explicit: active session management is adjacent, not core scope for agenttrace.
- README/Roadmap wording continues to favor diagnostic evidence and local-first reporting.
- Future parser opportunities from these tools require concrete local log/storage evidence before implementation issues are created.

## Suggested lane

lane/radar

## Risk

Medium. The user need is real, but copying active-session dashboards would pull agenttrace away from its lighter terminal-first diagnostic path.

## Source

- https://octoally.com/
- https://github.com/ai-genius-automations/octoally
- https://nimbalyst.com/mobile-agent-management/
- https://happy.engineering/docs/guides/happy-coder-best-practices/

## Background

A recent Codex VS Code extension issue reports prompt lag while local logs rapidly fill with repeated telemetry 403 errors and broadcast warnings. agenttrace already parses Codex CLI session files, but this signal suggests there may be a separate local diagnostic surface for Codex VS Code extension failures.

## Evidence

- Source issue: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/19371
- Reported symptom: prompt input becomes laggy while the extension/app-server log grows quickly.
- Reported log patterns include repeated `403 /ces/v1/rgstr` telemetry errors and `Received broadcast but no handler is configured` warnings.
- Tavily ecosystem scan on 2026-05-03 surfaced the issue while searching for Codex CLI/session debugging and tool-failure signals.
- No existing agenttrace issue matched `Codex VS Code telemetry logs` during duplicate search.

## User value

Users debugging slow or noisy Codex sessions should be able to distinguish session-level model/tool issues from extension-side telemetry/log spam when local evidence is available.

## Adoption rationale

A clear diagnostic boundary improves developer experience for Codex users: agenttrace can stay local-first while helping users understand whether the actionable evidence is in session traces, extension logs, or both.

## Suggested scope

- Verify whether Codex VS Code extension logs are locally accessible in a stable path and whether they contain enough structured evidence to summarize safely.
- Decide whether this belongs in parser support, doctor diagnostics, or documentation only.
- If local log parsing is considered, start with counting repeated error patterns and surfacing sanitized diagnostics rather than importing raw prompts or full logs.
- Keep the existing Codex CLI session parser behavior unchanged.

## Non-goals

- Do not upload logs or telemetry.
- Do not parse or expose raw prompt/session contents from extension logs.
- Do not implement a remote observability backend.
- Do not claim support for this source before a stable local fixture is available.

## Acceptance criteria

- Maintainer decides whether Codex VS Code extension log noise is in scope for agenttrace.
- If in scope, a follow-up parser or quality issue identifies the local log path, minimal fields, privacy boundary, and fixture requirement.
- If out of scope, docs or issue notes explain that Codex CLI session parsing remains the supported Codex path.
- Any future implementation avoids raw prompt/log upload and keeps diagnostics local.

lane/radar

title: [Radar] Track GitHub Copilot CLI session usage diagnostics
body:
## Background

GitHub Copilot CLI now documents session-oriented commands and state that overlap with agenttrace's local diagnostic vocabulary. The docs describe resuming interactive sessions, viewing context usage, and inspecting per-session usage statistics, while agenttrace currently only claims Copilot-style log support through parsed trace-like events.

- The docs describe `--resume`, `/resume`, and `copilot --continue` for returning to local interactive sessions.
- The docs describe `/usage` as showing session duration, edited lines, and token usage by model.
- The docs describe `/context` as a visual overview of current token usage.
- The docs note MCP server configuration under `~/.copilot` by default, with `COPILOT_HOME` as an override.
- Existing agenttrace PR #27 covered Copilot-style OpenTelemetry attribute maps, not Copilot CLI session usage or context diagnostics.

## User value

Copilot CLI users should know whether agenttrace can inspect their local session evidence, and if not, what exact fixture or export format would be needed before support is considered.

## Adoption rationale

Clarifying this boundary improves compatibility value and onboarding clarity for developers comparing local coding-agent diagnostics across Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Aider, and Copilot surfaces.

## Suggested scope

- Verify whether Copilot CLI exposes a stable local session history, usage export, or redacted fixture that can map to agenttrace sessions.
- Distinguish Copilot CLI session diagnostics from existing Copilot-style OpenTelemetry attribute parsing.
- Identify the minimum safe fields needed: session id, model, duration, token usage, context usage, edited-line count, tool/MCP activity if available, and timestamp.
- Keep this as a radar decision until a stable local fixture or documented export exists.

## Non-goals

- Do not parse private Copilot data without an explicit local fixture.
- Do not upload session, prompt, token, MCP, or tool logs.
- Do not claim GitHub Copilot CLI support in README or release notes before implementation exists.
- Do not replace the existing Copilot-style OpenTelemetry parser.

## Acceptance criteria

- Maintainer decides whether GitHub Copilot CLI session usage diagnostics are in scope.
- If in scope, a follow-up parser issue identifies the fixture/export path, field mapping, privacy boundary, and tests.
- If out of scope, release and README wording remain limited to currently implemented Copilot-style trace support.

lane/radar

- Do not infer a stable schema from one blog post alone.
- Do not change README parser coverage until implementation and validation land.

## Acceptance criteria

- Maintainer decides whether to keep this as active radar or close until user-submitted fixtures appear.
- At least one candidate tool has a minimal redacted/synthetic fixture or official schema-level documentation before implementation is scoped.

title: [Quality] Make demo overview ordering deterministic across output formats
body:
## Background

Product validation found that demo overview output can present `recent_sessions` and recent anomalies in different orders across repeated runs and output formats. The metric values are correct, but unstable ordering makes demo screenshots, README examples, PR artifacts, and CI comparisons harder to trust.

## Evidence

Validation on `agenttrace v0.3.46`:

- `agenttrace --demo --overview -f json` showed `recent_sessions` ordered as `03-shallow-chat`, `02-hanging-loop`, `01-healthy-ship`.
- `agenttrace --demo --overview -f markdown` showed `recent_sessions` ordered as `02-hanging-loop`, `01-healthy-ship`, `03-shallow-chat` on a repeated run.
- `agenttrace --demo --overview -f html -o /tmp/agenttrace-demo.html` showed HTML `Recent sessions` ordering changing between runs, including `02-hanging-loop`, `01-healthy-ship`, `03-shallow-chat` and later `03-shallow-chat`, `02-hanging-loop`, `01-healthy-ship`.
- Recent anomaly ordering also differed between JSON/Markdown/HTML runs.
- Duplicate checks for `recent sessions order HTML` and `overview order` found no existing issue.

## User value

Users comparing CLI, Markdown, HTML, and CI artifacts should see the same logical ordering for the same demo data, so differences reflect real product behavior rather than incidental iteration order.

## Adoption rationale

Deterministic report ordering improves Reliability value and Developer experience for onboarding screenshots, release validation, documentation examples, and automated artifact review.

## Suggested scope

- Define a deterministic ordering for overview recent sessions, for example by session timestamp/name or by the same canonical order used by JSON output.
- Apply the same ordering before rendering JSON, Markdown, and HTML overview outputs.
- Define deterministic ordering for recent anomalies as well.
- Add focused validation so repeated demo overview runs produce stable row order for all supported overview formats.

## Non-goals

- Do not change metric calculations.
- Do not change anomaly detection thresholds.
- Do not redesign report layout.
- Do not add new CLI flags.
- Do not change parser behavior.

## Acceptance criteria

- Repeated `agenttrace --demo --overview -f json` runs produce the same `recent_sessions` and anomaly order.
- Repeated `agenttrace --demo --overview -f markdown` runs produce the same row order as the canonical order.
- Repeated `agenttrace --demo --overview -f html` runs produce the same table order as the canonical order.
- Existing summary metrics remain unchanged for the demo dataset.
- Tests or golden assertions cover ordering for at least one representative overview dataset.

## Suggested lane

lane/quality, priority/P2, status/ready-for-agent

title: [Radar] Track upstream session-log fidelity gaps for cost and tool failures
body:
## Background

External agent ecosystems keep surfacing a shared reliability gap: local session logs are useful, but some tools either omit cost details, undercount usage, or report tool failures without enough error context. agenttrace should track this as a radar item before deciding whether parser warnings, docs notes, or fixture work are needed.

## Evidence

- Claude Code issue #23254 reports subagent token usage is shown by `/cost` but not persisted to local session JSONL, which limits downstream local reporting: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/23254
- Claude Code issue #27361 reports JSONL transcripts can miss final message stop events, making output token counts unreliable for local cost tools: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/27361
- Claude Code issue #55430 shows large repeated tool outputs and full-file writes dominating token usage in a real session, with transcript-size evidence: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/55430
- Claude Code issue #51218 reports prompt-cache expiry during active sessions causing sudden token spikes after idle periods: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/51218
- Codex issue #2420 reports the CLI can show `tool failed` while local logs do not include the underlying error detail: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/2420
- Duplicate checks for `Claude Code JSONL token usage subagent cost`, `tool failure logs Codex CLI`, `cache token spike Claude Code`, and `session log fidelity upstream cost accounting` found no exact open issue in this repository.

## User value

Users reading local reports need to know when a metric is derived from complete local evidence versus when the upstream session log may be missing cost, failure, or final-output details.

## Adoption rationale

Clear confidence boundaries improve Developer experience and Reliability value. They help users trust agenttrace reports while avoiding false precision when an upstream tool did not persist enough evidence.

## Suggested scope

- Keep this as radar until at least one minimal public fixture or reproducible local sample is available.
- Decide whether agenttrace should add parser-level confidence notes for known upstream log gaps.
- Decide whether docs should mention source-specific limitations for cost and tool-failure attribution.
- If fixture evidence becomes available, split concrete parser or product issues by source tool.

## Non-goals

- Do not infer private billing data that is not present in local logs.
- Do not upload or request user transcripts.
- Do not change parser behavior without fixture-backed evidence.
- Do not treat unrelated model-routing or hosted observability products as direct requirements.

## Acceptance criteria

- Maintainer decides whether this remains radar, becomes docs guidance, or splits into parser/product issues.
- Any follow-up issue names the source tool and the specific missing or unreliable field.
- Follow-up acceptance criteria require local fixture evidence or a reproducible public sample.
- agenttrace public copy avoids overclaiming exact cost attribution where the upstream log is known to be incomplete.

## Suggested lane

lane/radar, priority/P2, status/needs-human

## Risk

Medium. Overreacting could add noisy warnings; ignoring the signal could make reports look more precise than the underlying logs support.

## Source

- The updated list begins with entries such as `databricks-gpt-oss-120b`, `router`, and long provider-specific names, while common user-facing models are not prioritized on the first screen.

- Decide whether updated pricing output should be sorted, grouped, capped, filtered, or split from the compact supported-model view.

title: [Quality] Align TUI and overview/export aggregate metrics
body:
## Background

Full local validation of `agenttrace v0.3.48` found that the TUI and overview exports report materially different aggregate metrics for the same machine and same installed version.

agenttrace is positioned as local-first observability for AI coding agent sessions. If the TUI, JSON, Markdown, and HTML surfaces disagree on sessions, tokens, cost, health, or critical counts, users cannot trust the product as an operational source of truth.

## Evidence

Validation environment:

- Installed binary: `agenttrace v0.3.48`
- Command used for TUI: `agenttrace`
- Command used for export: `agenttrace --overview -f json`
- Doctor reported `Session files: 4250`
- Local data sources included Hermes Agent, Codex CLI, Codex archived sessions, Claude Code, and Gemini tmp sessions.

Observed TUI overview values:

```text
4250 sessions
681.3M tokens
$4233.68 cost
2.62% errors
77% health
297 critical sessions
```

Observed JSON overview summary from the same installed version:

```json
{
  "total_sessions": 1695,
  "total_tokens": 8189251600,
  "total_cost": 4380.2157,
  "avg_health": 90.1817,
  "critical": 35,
  "tool_fail_rate": 1.6355
}
```

Observed Markdown overview also used the export-style numbers, for example:

```text
Sessions: 1695
Average health: 90.2
Money Wasted: $4383.34
Total tokens: 8194316872
Tool failures: 1842 / 112682 (1.6%)
```

## User value

Users should be able to compare the TUI, JSON, Markdown, and HTML artifacts without wondering which one is authoritative.

## Suggested scope

- Identify why the TUI counts 4250 sessions while overview export counts 1695 sessions.
- Align aggregate metric calculation across TUI, JSON, Markdown, and HTML output.
- Define and document whether "sessions" means discovered files, parsed sessions, valid sessions, or reportable sessions.
- Apply the same aggregation source to total tokens, cost, average health, critical count, and tool failure rate.

## Non-goals

- Do not redesign the TUI layout.
- Do not change parser semantics unless required to fix the aggregation contract.
- Do not expose private prompt or session content in tests or fixtures.

## Acceptance criteria

- For the same dataset, TUI, JSON, Markdown, and HTML report the same values for sessions, tokens, cost, health, critical count, and tool failure rate.
- If discovered files and parsed/reportable sessions are intentionally different, the TUI labels them separately.
- Regression tests cover the shared aggregation contract.
- A large mixed-source dataset does not produce divergent aggregate totals across output formats.

## Risk

High user-trust risk. The product can still run, but conflicting metrics undermine the core observability promise.

## Source

Local product validation of `agenttrace v0.3.48` on May 4, 2026. No private prompt or session content is included in this issue.

title: [Quality] Prevent loop waste from exceeding total session cost
body:
## Background

Full TUI validation of `agenttrace v0.3.48` found a detail/diagnostics cost explanation where loop waste was shown as greater than the total session cost.

This breaks the cost narrative in the product. A user can accept estimated costs, but the displayed relationship between total cost and waste must be internally consistent.

## Evidence

Validation environment:

- Installed binary: `agenttrace v0.3.48`
- Command used: `agenttrace`
- Flow: TUI overview -> critical sessions -> detail -> diagnostics
- Source data: local AI coding agent session logs

Observed detail card for one real local session:

```text
HEALTH 46/100
COST $0.0008
TOOLS 4/5 80%
Model deepseek-v4-pro
```

Observed detail insight:

```text
Impact: Loop waste is $0.0750 of $0.0008 total (9375%) — consider adding circuit breaker
```

Observed diagnostics insight:

```text
Simple loop detected (cost $0.0750)
```

The statement `$0.0750 of $0.0008 total` is mathematically inconsistent if loop waste is a subset of the total session cost.

## User value

Cost explanations should help users trust and act on agenttrace findings. Inconsistent cost math makes the TUI look unreliable even when the underlying anomaly detection may be useful.

## Suggested scope

- Audit loop waste cost calculation and display formatting.
- Decide whether loop waste is actual session cost, projected opportunity cost, estimated retry cost, or another derived metric.
- If it is a subset of total cost, clamp or calculate it so it never exceeds total session cost.
- If it is not a subset, label it clearly as projected or estimated opportunity cost and avoid phrasing it as "of total".
- Align Detail and Diagnostics wording.

## Non-goals

- Do not remove loop detection.
- Do not hide cost insights entirely.
- Do not change pricing data unless that is the root cause.

## Acceptance criteria

- Loop waste is never displayed as greater than total cost when phrased as part of the total.
- If loop waste can exceed total cost by design, the UI labels it as projected or estimated opportunity cost.
- Detail and Diagnostics use the same cost semantics.
- A regression test covers a low-total-cost loop session.

## Risk

High user-trust risk. This directly affects one of the product's strongest value propositions: finding cost waste.

## Source

Local TUI validation of `agenttrace v0.3.48` on May 4, 2026. No private prompt or session content is included in this issue.

title: [Quality] Make demo latest session selection deterministic

## Background

README presents `agenttrace --latest`, `agenttrace --latest -f json`, and `agenttrace --latest --lang zh` as user-facing smoke-test and reporting commands. Product validation found that the built-in demo `--latest` path can select different demo sessions across repeated runs, so first-time users may see different health, cost, model, and anomaly evidence for the same command.

## Evidence

Local validation on 2026-05-04 with `agenttrace v0.3.46`:

- Repeated `agenttrace --demo --latest -f json` runs returned different sessions:
  - run 1: estimated cost `0.057`, model `gemini-2.5-pro`, anomalies `2`
  - run 3: estimated cost `0.7113`, model `gpt-5.1`, anomalies `3`
- Repeated `agenttrace --demo --latest --lang zh -f json` runs also varied:
  - run 1: estimated cost `0.0423`, model `claude-sonnet-4`, anomalies `0`
  - run 2: estimated cost `0.057`, model `gemini-2.5-pro`, anomalies `2`
  - run 4: estimated cost `0.7113`, model `gpt-5.1`, anomalies `3`
- Text output shows the same instability across repeated runs, with cost/model/health changing between demo sessions.
- README examples include `agenttrace --latest`, `agenttrace --latest -f json`, and `agenttrace --latest --lang zh`.
- Duplicate checks for `demo latest nondeterministic`, `latest ordering deterministic demo`, `--latest different session repeated runs`, and `deterministic latest session` found no exact open issue. #93 is related to release/demo packaging but does not cover latest-session selection determinism.

## User value

Users running the same demo or smoke-test command should get stable evidence, so differences reflect product changes rather than incidental session ordering.

## Adoption rationale

Deterministic `--latest` output improves Reliability value and Developer experience for onboarding, support screenshots, README smoke tests, localized output checks, and automated JSON comparisons.

## Suggested scope

- Define a deterministic latest-session tie breaker for demo and regular discovery paths, such as timestamp, name, and path.
- Apply the same selection path across text, JSON, and localized output.
- Add focused tests or fixture validation for repeated `--demo --latest` runs.
- Confirm behavior after any existing overview ordering logic from #104, without expanding scope into report layout or cost wording.

## Non-goals

- Do not change health, cost, anomaly, or parser calculations.
- Do not change report formatting beyond the selected session.
- Do not change localized wording.
- Do not bundle this with release packaging or sample report version alignment.

## Acceptance criteria

- Repeated `agenttrace --demo --latest` runs select the same demo session.
- Repeated `agenttrace --demo --latest -f json` runs select the same demo session.
- Repeated `agenttrace --demo --latest --lang zh` runs select the same demo session as the non-localized path.
- The deterministic choice is documented in tests or implementation comments where useful.
- Existing summary metrics and anomaly calculations for the selected session remain unchanged.

## Suggested lane

lane/quality, priority/P2, status/ready-for-agent

## Risk

Low to medium. The main risk is unintentionally changing what real users consider "latest" when timestamps tie or session metadata is missing. Keep the change limited to deterministic tie breaking and preserve existing semantics where ordering is already unambiguous.

## Background

Full local validation of `agenttrace v0.3.48` found confusing cache feedback between the TUI footer and `agenttrace --doctor`.

The product already has an incremental cache story, and it matters for large local datasets. On a machine with thousands of session files, users need to understand whether startup is parsing from scratch or loading from cache.

## Evidence

Validation environment:

- Installed binary: `agenttrace v0.3.48`
- Command used for TUI: `agenttrace`
- Command used for diagnostics: `agenttrace --doctor`
- Doctor reported `Session files: 4250`

Observed doctor cache status:

```text
Cache: /Users/edy/Library/Caches/agenttrace/sessions.json
  4245 entries, 4244 valid for current scan, 368 cached directories
```

Observed TUI footer after full load:

```text
Overview · 4250/4250 · cache 0/4250
```

Observed TUI behavior on a second launch still started from a progressive loading state and showed `cache 0/...` while loading.

## User value

Users with large session directories should know whether agenttrace is benefiting from cached parsing. The current footer makes it look like the cache is unused even when doctor reports many valid cache entries.

## Suggested scope

- Align the TUI cache footer with the same cache validity semantics used by doctor.
- Distinguish discovered files, parsed sessions, cache entries, and cache hits if those are different concepts.
- Make second-launch cache behavior visibly faster or visibly cache-backed for large datasets.
- Consider showing `cache hits / valid cache entries` instead of `cache 0/total` if that is the intended meaning.

## Non-goals

- Do not remove progressive loading.
- Do not change the cache file location unless necessary.
- Do not expose local file contents in the UI.

## Acceptance criteria

- TUI footer cache numbers match or clearly map to doctor cache status.
- On a large local dataset, a second launch visibly reflects cache usage.
- Doctor and TUI use consistent terms for cache entries, valid entries, and hits.
- Regression tests cover footer rendering for cached and uncached states.

## Risk

Medium. The core product still works, but unclear cache feedback weakens perceived performance and reliability.

## Source

Local validation of `agenttrace v0.3.48` on May 4, 2026. No private prompt or session content is included in this issue.

title: [Product] Improve large-dataset TUI list scanability
body:
## Background

Full local TUI validation of `agenttrace v0.3.48` on a large dataset found that the session list works, but it becomes hard to scan when thousands of sessions and many source/model names are present.

The TUI successfully loaded thousands of local session files, which is a strong capability. The next product improvement is to help users summarize and navigate that dataset without reading dense rows one by one.

## Evidence

Validation environment:

- Installed binary: `agenttrace v0.3.48`
- Command used: `agenttrace`
- Doctor reported `Session files: 4250`
- TUI loaded a large mixed-source dataset with Hermes Agent, Codex CLI, Claude Code, and other session sources.

Observed list behavior:

- The critical filter showed `297/4250 sessions`.
- The list was dense and useful, but source/model/session columns were often truncated.
- The user could see per-row health, cost, tokens, failures, and anomaly type, but it was hard to answer higher-level questions such as "which source is driving most critical sessions?" or "which model is producing the most failures?" from the list alone.
- The TUI headline used `sessions` for what may include discovered files, while exports used a smaller parsed/reportable session count.

## User value

Users with large local agent histories need a fast way to move from thousands of rows to the highest-impact source, model, or failure class.

## Suggested scope

Consider adding one or more large-dataset affordances:

- A source/model aggregation toggle in the TUI.
- Column explanations or a compact legend for truncated headers and metrics.
- A top-line distinction between discovered files, parsed sessions, and visible/reportable sessions.
- A grouping mode by source, model, health band, or anomaly type.
- A shortcut to jump from an aggregate group into filtered rows.

## Non-goals

- Do not remove the existing row-level session list.
- Do not expose private prompt or message content.
- Do not add a hosted backend or remote telemetry.

## Acceptance criteria

- On a dataset with thousands of sessions, the TUI helps users identify the dominant source/model/anomaly driver without manually scanning many pages of rows.
- The TUI clearly distinguishes parsed sessions from discovered files if those counts differ.
- Existing row-level filters and detail navigation continue to work.
- The UI remains readable at a standard terminal size.

## Risk

Medium. This is primarily product/UX work, but it affects the first impression for power users with large local datasets.

## Source

Local TUI validation of `agenttrace v0.3.48` on May 4, 2026. No private prompt or session content is included in this issue.

title: [Product] Polish TUI loading, diff empty state, and command feedback
body:
## Background

Full TUI validation of `agenttrace v0.3.48` found that the core interaction model works, but several small interaction details can be improved.

These are not blockers, but they would make the TUI feel more responsive and easier to understand, especially during large local scans.

## Evidence

Validation flows:

- `agenttrace --demo`
- `agenttrace`
- Overview -> critical sessions -> detail -> diagnostics -> diff empty state
- Help/keymap view
- Command mode with `:sort cost desc`
- Large local dataset loading with more than 4000 discovered session files

Observed behavior:

- Pressing `q` during large dataset loading did not feel immediate; the TUI appeared to wait for the current loading batch before exiting.
- Diff view correctly showed `Need at least two visible sessions to compare` when only one filtered session was visible, but it did not suggest how to recover, such as clearing the filter or returning to the list.
- Command mode worked for `:sort cost desc`, but command feedback and mode transitions can be hard to follow across different views.

## User value

Small interaction improvements make the TUI feel more reliable and reduce user confusion during triage.

## Suggested scope

- Make `q` during loading respond as quickly as possible.
- Improve the diff empty state with an actionable hint, for example: clear filters, return to list, or select another visible session.
- Make command mode feedback consistent across overview, list, detail, diagnostics, and diff views.
- Consider showing a transient confirmation when commands change view, filter, or sort state.

## Non-goals

- Do not redesign the whole TUI navigation model.
- Do not remove keyboard-first interaction.
- Do not change metric calculations.

## Acceptance criteria

- `q` exits promptly during large dataset loading.
- Diff empty state explains why comparison is unavailable and how to recover.
- Command mode feedback is visible and consistent across all major TUI views.
- Existing shortcuts such as `!`, `$`, `w`, `d`, `?`, `:`, and `Enter` continue to work.

## Risk

Low to medium. These are polish items, but they affect perceived responsiveness and UX quality.

title: [Quality] Add local trace evidence to failed health-gate output
body:
## Background

Maintainer direction on #99 approved promoting the trace-first CI / tool-recovery radar into a concrete feature. The smallest useful workflow is not a new eval framework; it is making a failed local health gate more explainable with evidence agenttrace already computes.

## User value

When a CI or local gate fails, users should quickly see why: low average health, critical sessions, high tool-failure rate, and the local report or session evidence that helps them inspect the bad run.

## Scope

Add a concise evidence section to failed health-gate output that points to existing local facts, for example:

- failed threshold and observed value;
- critical session count;
- tool-failure rate;
- relevant local report/session path when available;
- next command that produces a JSON or HTML report for inspection.

Prefer using existing overview/gate data. Keep the output deterministic and compact.

## Non-goals

- Do not add an eval framework, remote judge, hosted trace storage, or behavioral fingerprinting.
- Do not upload traces or prompt content.
- Do not change pass/fail thresholds unless a compatibility review explicitly requires it.
- Do not claim regression-detection support beyond the implemented evidence output.

## Acceptance criteria

- A failing gate includes a small local-evidence explanation for the failure.
- Passing gate behavior remains unchanged or only receives compatible wording cleanup.
- Existing JSON/HTML report contracts remain stable unless intentionally versioned.
- Add or update focused fixture coverage for failing gate output.
- These checks pass: `go test ./...`, `scripts/ci/check-output-contract.sh`, `scripts/ci/check-deterministic-output.sh`, `scripts/ci/check-report-semantics.sh`, and `scripts/ci/check-docs-commands.sh`.

title: feat: add support for pi coding agent sessions (earendil-works/pi)
body:
## Summary

Adds support for parsing **pi** (earendil-works/pi) coding agent session files. pi is the most popular AI coding agent CLI with **46k+ GitHub stars**, and this adds agentwaste analysis capabilities for its JSONL session format.

## What's New

- **`parser_pi.go`** — Full parser for pi's JSONL session format
  - Supports all entry types: `session`, `message`, `model_change`, `compaction`, `branch_summary`, `thinking_level_change`, `session_info`
  - Handles all message roles: `user`, `assistant`, `toolResult`, `bashExecution`, `compactionSummary`, `branchSummary`
  - Parses Anthropic-compatible content blocks: `text`, `thinking`, `toolCall` (camelCase), `image`
  - Extracts embedded usage/cost data from pi assistant messages (pi includes full pricing info!)
  - Converts dual-format timestamps (ISO strings + Unix ms numbers)

- **Format Detection** — Two detection paths:
  - **JSONL detection**: first line `{"type":"session","version":3,...}` → pi
  - **Single-JSON fallback**: Go's `json.Unmarshal` parses the first JSONL line as a single object → `detectSingleJSON` now recognizes pi headers

- **`parser_pi_test.go`** — 8 test cases covering:
  - Basic session with user/assistant/toolCall/toolResult flow
  - Thinking content blocks
  - Model change events
  - Compaction entries
  - Empty/invalid input handling
  - Format detection via temp file

## How It Works

pi sessions are JSONL files stored at `~/.pi/agent/sessions/`. Each line is a JSON object with a `type` field:

```
{"type":"session","version":3,"id":"...","cwd":"/project",...}
{"type":"message","message":{"role":"user","content":[{type:"text",...}]}}
{"type":"message","message":{"role":"assistant","content":[{type:"toolCall",...}],"usage":{...},"model":"..."}}
{"type":"message","message":{"role":"toolResult","toolCallId":"...","content":[...],"isError":false}}
```

The parser linearizes the tree structure (id/parentId) for analysis — all events are produced in file order.

## Test Plan

- [x] 8 new unit tests all pass
- [x] All 23 existing tests still pass (no regressions)
- [x] `go vet` clean
- [x] Binary builds and successfully analyzes real pi session files
- [x] Manual verification with actual pi session data from badlogicgames/pi-mono

title: Design incident timeline and tool-authority signals for agent debugging
body:
## Background

A new external Discussion #2 comment asks for agenttrace to make daily debugging less dependent on a generic health score and more oriented around incident reconstruction and CI regression review.

## Evidence

- Discussion #2 comment from `armorer-labs` on 2026-05-12 requests a first-screen incident timeline with: last successful user-visible milestone, longest idle gap and preceding event, repeated tool failure loops grouped by tool and normalized error, files/tools touched since the last checkpoint, and the first point where cost/token burn diverged from the session baseline.
- The same comment says the strongest CI gate use case is regression testing scripted agent workflows: whether a task became slower, more expensive, more failure-prone, or touched a broader file/tool surface than last week.
- The comment also asks for tool authority/safety metadata that separates read-only file access, test runs, package installs, shell execution, git writes, and external network calls.
- Duplicate check on 2026-05-17 found no open issue for `incident timeline tool authority CI regression`, `tool authority safety metadata`, `CI regression workflow slower expensive failure-prone`, or `idle gap checkpoint tool failure loop`.

## User value

Users debugging real agent runs need a compact explanation of what changed, where the run got stuck, and whether the agent crossed higher-risk tool boundaries, not just a single score.

## Adoption rationale

This turns community feedback into a clearer product direction for daily debugging and CI evidence. It strengthens agenttrace's local-first session observability positioning by focusing on actionable incident reconstruction and repeatable workflow regression checks.

## Suggested scope

- Design a first-screen or report-level incident timeline that summarizes milestone, idle-gap, retry-loop, touched-surface, and burn-divergence evidence.
- Define a CI regression comparison shape for scripted agent workflows, including time, cost/token, failure-loop, and file/tool-surface drift.
- Define tool authority/safety categories for local reports, such as read-only access, tests, package installs, shell execution, git writes, and network calls.
- Start with product/spec acceptance before implementation so parser and quality owners can split the work safely.

## Non-goals

- Do not add hosted telemetry or remote log upload.
- Do not turn the health score into a compliance or security certification.
- Do not require billing-grade cost accounting.
- Do not change package or release state.
- Do not publish external announcements from this task.

## Acceptance criteria

- A proposed UX/report shape explains how incident timeline evidence appears in TUI and exported reports.
- A proposed CI regression contract identifies which fields can be compared between runs without relying on private uploaded state.
- Tool authority categories are defined clearly enough for Quality/Parser follow-up tasks.
- The proposal cites Discussion #2 feedback and stays consistent with local-first positioning.

## Suggested lane

lane/product

## Risk

Medium. The main risk is over-scoping into security policy or live tracing. Keep the first version focused on local post-run evidence and CI-friendly comparisons.

## Source

Product review of Discussion #2 on 2026-05-17: https://github.com/luoyuctl/agenttrace/discussions/2#discussioncomment-16895719

title: Add local baseline comparison for CI agent workflow regressions
body:
## Background

Issue #198 defined a first-version product contract for comparing scripted agent workflow runs in CI without requiring hosted state.

## Evidence

- Discussion #2 feedback says the strongest CI gate use case is regression testing agent workflows: detecting whether a scripted task became slower, more expensive, more failure-prone, or touched a broader file/tool surface than a previous run.
- #198 proposes baseline-report comparison fields such as elapsed time, token/cost deltas, new failure families, broader tool/file surface, and new high-authority tool use.
- Duplicate search on 2026-05-17 found no separate open task for baseline report comparison.

## User value

Users running scripted agent tasks in CI should be able to detect regressions across runs, not only evaluate one current report in isolation.

## Adoption rationale

Repeatable CI evidence makes agenttrace more useful for teams that need to review agent workflow drift over time while keeping all artifacts local or inside their own CI system.

## Suggested scope

- Define and implement a local baseline comparison mode for agenttrace report artifacts.
- Support comparing two local JSON reports, or a current report plus a baseline file supplied by CI.
- Emit deterministic JSON fields suitable for thresholds: slower_than_baseline, cost_delta_pct, token_delta_pct, new_failure_families, broader_tool_surface, broader_file_surface, and new_high_authority_tool_use.
- Keep thresholds explicit in CLI flags or config.

## Non-goals

- Do not add hosted storage or remote state.
- Do not invent hidden policy thresholds.
- Do not require billing-grade cost reconciliation.
- Do not change package/release state.

## Acceptance criteria

- A CI workflow can compare a current report against a local baseline artifact.
- JSON output exposes deterministic regression fields for time, cost/tokens, failures, and touched surface.
- Missing baseline or incompatible report versions produce clear diagnostics.
- Existing output-contract, deterministic-output, and report-semantics checks are extended or preserved.

## Suggested lane

lane/quality

## Risk

Medium. Baseline comparison can become noisy if thresholds are implicit or unstable; keep comparison fields explicit and deterministic.

## Source

Follow-up split from #198 and Discussion #2 feedback: https://github.com/luoyuctl/agenttrace/discussions/2#discussioncomment-16895719

title: Classify tool authority categories in local session reports
body:
## Background

Issue #198 defines tool authority/safety categories so reports can show whether an agent session crossed higher-risk tool boundaries.

## Evidence

- Discussion #2 feedback says tool calls should not all be treated equally and asks for separate counters for read-only file access, test runs, package installs, shell execution, git writes, and external network calls.
- #198 proposes initial categories: read_only_files, write_files, test_or_build, package_install, shell_exec, git_write, network_access, external_publish, and unknown_authority.
- Duplicate search on 2026-05-17 found no separate open task for tool authority categories.

## User value

Users reviewing an agent session should be able to see the highest-risk boundary reached and whether a new run used broader or riskier tools than expected.

## Adoption rationale

Tool authority summaries improve trust in local reports and make CI review more actionable without turning agenttrace into a hosted security product.

## Suggested scope

- Add a shared best-effort tool authority classifier for local reports.
- Classify tool calls into the initial categories from #198.
- Surface counts by category and the highest category reached in report/TUI data where appropriate.
- Treat unknown or ambiguous tool calls conservatively as unknown_authority rather than under-classifying.
- Leave source-specific parser mapping as follow-up if a source lacks enough tool metadata.

## Non-goals

- Do not claim security certification or policy enforcement.
- Do not block commands by default.
- Do not upload logs or tool data to a hosted service.
- Do not require perfect classification for every source in the first pass.

## Acceptance criteria

- Reports expose tool authority category counts and highest category reached when tool metadata is available.
- Unknown or ambiguous tool calls are represented explicitly.
- Classification is deterministic for fixtures.
- CI/report checks can later compare whether a run introduced a new high-authority category.

## Suggested lane

lane/quality

## Risk

Medium. Classification can be misleading if it is too confident. Prefer conservative categories and explicit unknowns.

## Source

Follow-up split from #198 and Discussion #2 feedback: https://github.com/luoyuctl/agenttrace/discussions/2#discussioncomment-16895719

## Background

#205 added tool authority classification to overview data so users can see whether a session used read-only, test/build, or higher-authority tool surfaces. The JSON overview now exposes this through `summary.tool_authority`, `surfaces.authority_categories`, `surfaces.high_authority_tools`, and per-session `highest_tool_authority`.

The HTML overview is the shareable/readable report surface, but the current generated HTML does not make that authority summary visible.

## Evidence

Validated on master `1c13313` after #208:

- `go build -o /tmp/agenttrace-product-check ./cmd/agenttrace` passed.
- `/tmp/agenttrace-product-check --demo --overview -f json` includes `summary.tool_authority`, `surfaces.authority_categories`, `surfaces.high_authority_tools`, and `recent_sessions[].highest_tool_authority`.
- `/tmp/agenttrace-product-check --demo --overview -f html -o /tmp/agenttrace-demo.html` renders Health Trend, Incident timeline, Recent sessions, By agent, By model, and Recent anomalies, but does not render a visible tool authority / authority category summary.
- `scripts/ci/check-report-semantics.sh` validates the JSON authority fields, but no current check appears to require the HTML report to render them.

## User value

A user reading the HTML report should not have to inspect JSON to answer whether a slow or risky run touched higher-authority tools. This is especially useful when sharing local evidence with teammates through an exported HTML report.

## Adoption rationale

The report becomes easier to understand as a standalone artifact: local-first evidence, incident timeline, baseline comparison, and tool authority can all be evaluated from the readable HTML surface.

## Suggested scope

Render a concise tool authority summary in `agenttrace --overview -f html`, using existing computed overview data.

A minimal shape is enough:

- highest authority category;
- authority category counts;
- high-authority tools, when any exist;
- optional per-session authority column if it stays readable.

Add or extend a repeatable check so the demo HTML overview cannot silently drop this summary again.

## Non-goals

- Do not change authority classification rules.
- Do not add hosted telemetry, upload, or external sharing behavior.
- Do not change JSON field names or existing report contracts unless there is a separate compatibility decision.
- Do not make release, package, npm, or Homebrew changes.

## Acceptance criteria

- `agenttrace --demo --overview -f html -o /tmp/agenttrace-demo.html` includes a visible tool authority summary when authority data exists.
- JSON overview output remains compatible with the existing authority fields.

title: Make text overview truncation Unicode-safe
body:
## Background

Text overview is now a stronger first-run surface after #214: it shows incident timeline and tool authority cues directly in the terminal. Some text rows still truncate strings by byte index, which can split multibyte session names or tool labels when local paths, project names, or prompts contain non-ASCII characters.

## Evidence

On current master `5a48c9d`:

- `internal/engine/report.go` truncates recent anomaly session names with `name[:30]`.
- `internal/engine/report.go` helper `textCell` truncates with `value[:limit-3] + "..."`.
- `textCell` is now used for incident timeline session names/details and high-authority tool lists in text overview.
- Existing report tests cover Chinese labels for Markdown/HTML, but text overview does not currently have a regression check for Unicode-safe truncation.

## User value

Users with non-English project/session names should get readable terminal output rather than broken UTF-8 bytes or replacement characters in the fastest overview path.

## Adoption rationale

The CLI first impression should be robust across local developer environments. This is especially relevant because agenttrace positions itself as local-first and source-agnostic across many agent tools and workspaces.

## Suggested scope

- Introduce or update a small truncation helper for text overview that preserves valid UTF-8/rune boundaries.
- Apply it to the recent anomalies row and the #214 text evidence rows.
- Add a focused regression test using a long non-ASCII session name and/or detail.
- Keep output compact; do not redesign text overview layout.

## Non-goals

- Do not change JSON, Markdown, or HTML report contracts.
- Do not change parser behavior or session discovery.
- Do not add new CLI flags.
- Do not touch release, package, npm, Homebrew, or public site surfaces.

## Acceptance criteria

- Text overview output remains valid UTF-8 when truncating long non-ASCII session/detail strings.
- Recent anomalies and incident timeline text rows use the same safe truncation behavior.
- Existing text overview #214 cues remain visible in demo output.

lane/product

body:
## Background

Google has announced that Gemini CLI users should migrate to Antigravity CLI. agenttrace currently lists Gemini CLI as a supported local coding-agent session source, so this transition is relevant to parser coverage, onboarding clarity, and future compatibility positioning.

This is only a radar item. There is not yet enough local trace evidence to create a parser or docs implementation task.

## Evidence

- Google Developers Blog announced `Transitioning Gemini CLI to Antigravity CLI` and states that Gemini CLI users can continue the workflow in Antigravity CLI: https://developers.googleblog.com/an-important-update-transitioning-gemini-cli-to-antigravity-cli/
- Google I/O 2026 developer highlights say Google encourages Gemini CLI users to migrate to Antigravity CLI: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/google-io-2026-developer-highlights/
- Duplicate check on 2026-05-20 for `Antigravity Gemini CLI transition parser` and `Gemini Antigravity` found no existing matching issue in this repository.

## User value

Users who currently expect Gemini CLI session coverage need a clear future answer about whether Antigravity CLI produces compatible local history, changed paths, changed event formats, or different tool/cost/session evidence.

## Adoption rationale

Tracking the transition early helps keep parser coverage and onboarding language aligned with the active coding-agent ecosystem without promising support before a real local artifact is verified.

## Suggested scope

- Keep this as radar until Antigravity CLI local session artifacts are available for inspection.
- Compare Antigravity CLI local history paths, event schema, tool-call records, token/cost fields, and session identity fields against existing Gemini CLI parsing.
- If promoted later, split into a narrow parser or docs task with a fixture-backed acceptance check.
- Keep existing Gemini CLI wording unless public evidence shows it has become misleading for active users.

## Non-goals

- Do not add Antigravity CLI parser support without a local fixture or reproducible sample.
- Do not remove Gemini CLI support from public docs based only on migration messaging.
- Do not claim Antigravity CLI compatibility before validating local artifacts.
- Do not create package, release, or external posting work from this radar item.

## Acceptance criteria

- Maintainer or future Product review decides whether this remains radar, becomes a parser task, or becomes a docs compatibility task.
- Any promoted task names the exact local artifact path or event schema being validated.
- Any parser work includes a minimal fixture or reproducible local sample.
- Public copy remains conservative and distinguishes existing verified Gemini CLI support from unverified Antigravity CLI compatibility.

## Suggested lane

lane/radar, priority/P2, status/needs-human

## Risk

Medium. The ecosystem signal is strong, but implementation risk is high without artifact-level evidence. Acting too early could introduce incorrect parser claims or confuse existing Gemini CLI users.

## Source

source/radar: ecosystem scan on 2026-05-20. Tavily MCP was not exposed in this session, so Product used search fallback and prioritized official Google sources.

title: Clarify doctor cache cold and reusable directory wording
body:
## Background

`agenttrace --doctor` is the first diagnostic path users run when they want to understand whether local session discovery and cache reuse are working. In the current local product check, the cache section reports both invalid current-scan entries and cached directories, then the recommendations say the cache is cold. That is probably technically correct, but it reads ambiguous for a user who is trying to decide whether startup will be fast on the next run.

## Evidence

Product validation on 2026-05-20 from clean `origin/master` build `d2a65f6`:

```text
AGENTTRACE Doctor
Version: 0.5.0
Mode: auto-discovery
Sessions: 2063
Cache: /Users/edy/Library/Caches/agenttrace/sessions.json
  1 entries, 0 valid for current scan, 362 cached directories
...
Recommendations:
  - Ready: run `agenttrace` for the TUI or `agenttrace --overview -f json` for automation.
  - Cache is cold for this scan. The next TUI startup should reuse parsed sessions incrementally.
```

Validation commands around this output passed:

```bash
go build -o /tmp/agenttrace-product-check ./cmd/agenttrace
go test ./...
/tmp/agenttrace-product-check --doctor || true
```

Duplicate checks for `doctor cache cold cached directories`, `cache doctor recommendations valid current scan`, and `doctor diagnostic clarity cache` found no matching open issue.

## User value

A clearer doctor cache explanation helps users understand whether agenttrace is healthy, whether the next startup should reuse cached parse work, and whether they need to clear or rebuild cache state.

## Adoption rationale

Doctor output is a high-trust onboarding and support surface. Small wording improvements reduce confusion without changing parser behavior or release surfaces.

## Suggested scope

- Keep behavior conservative; this is about diagnostic clarity unless implementation discovers a real bug.
- Clarify the relationship between total cache entries, valid entries for the current scan, cached directories, and the `cache cold` recommendation.
- If the current wording is intentionally precise, add a short explanation or rename the metric so users can tell what action, if any, is needed.
- Add or update focused test coverage for the doctor cache summary/recommendation if an existing test seam exists.

## Non-goals

- Do not change cache invalidation semantics unless a bug is proven.
- Do not clear or delete user cache files.
- Do not add new telemetry, hosted tracing, or uploaded logs.
- Do not create release, package, or external posting work from this issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- `agenttrace --doctor` explains cold-cache versus reusable cached directory state in user-facing language.
- Existing doctor/source discovery information remains present.
- `go test ./...` passes.
- Any docs or snapshots touched remain consistent with current v0.5.0 behavior.

## Suggested lane

lane/quality, priority/P2, status/ready-for-agent

## Risk

Low. The issue is narrow and limited to diagnostics wording, with a possible small test update.

## Source

source/product: post-release Product validation of the v0.5.0 doctor path on 2026-05-20.
